title: Which body carries a survey payload furthest per kWh? Hull choice for small autonomous boats
lede: research programme (proposal stage): energy per survey kilometre of hull types for 100 to 500 kg autonomous boats; with a Michell wave term a catamaran out-ranges a monohull in 3.3% of 6,561 cases, none at equal length; with Slocum coefficients from the gliderflight package a glider never out-ranges a same-mass propeller AUV at equal hotel load (0 of 2,430 cases); it breaks even when the AUV's hotel load is about 5 times its own; a REMUS-100-class AUV's non-propulsion load implied by vendor endurance is 104 to 175 W, far above that, so the glider out-ranges it in every case on energy per metre (at a tenth of the speed); a Savitsky planing hull reaches at most 0.14 of the monohull range (0 of 48 cases); a SWATH (two submerged torpedoes on struts) out-ranges the monohull in none of 4,374 swept pairs; charging panel mass to the battery (2 to 10 kg/m2, swept) cuts the median solar range multiplier from 2.01 to 1.64 at worst, and the full deck stays the best array wherever range is finite; against ten years of daily NASA POWER insolation a threshold speed policy (slow or hold when the pack is under 30%) never raises km/day over a fixed 1 m/s but cuts pack-empty days, e.g. 25.4% to 1.5% for a 4 m boat at 25 N
summary: An open research programme on which body (monohull, catamaran, SWATH, planing hull, hydrofoil, glider, AUV) carries a survey payload furthest per kWh, and where that ranking flips under uncertain drag inputs. Milestone 1 is a stdlib calculator (ITTC 1957 friction line checked analytically, form factor, wetted-area constant, hotel load; 9 tests) and a 6,561-case grid for a 200 kg craft: a catamaran of two slender demi-hulls out-ranges a monohull in 27 cases (0.4%) and in none of the 2,187 equal-length cases; the monohull's best speed is about 1 m/s, set by a 30 W hotel load, with range 560 to 1,188 km as an upper bound. The wave-resistance term is a placeholder and no published resistance curve is reproduced yet, so this is a friction-limited comparison; hull-form constants, efficiencies and water properties are swept or unsourced, and stability and deck area are not modelled. Two DOIs written from memory were wrong and were corrected by the citation check. Preliminary; simulation only. Milestone 2 replaces the placeholder wave term with Michell thin-ship theory on Wigley hulls: the catamaran wins 3.3% of 6,561 cases and none at equal length, and wave resistance changes best range by about 4% because the optimum speed (about 1 m/s) is at Froude number 0.16. Milestone 3a checks it against one published Wigley tank point (Ju 1983, via Wang et al. 2017): Michell plus the ITTC 1957 line with no form factor is within +1 to +5% of the measured total-resistance coefficient 4.16e-3 (water temperature unknown, 10 to 20 C), while the programme's central form factor 0.25 is 18 to 25% high; the form factor that fits is about 0, below the swept 0.10 to 0.40 box. One speed, second-hand source, geometry assumed. Milestone 4 compares a quasi-steady buoyancy glider with a same-mass propeller AUV over 19,683 swept cases (no glider coefficient is sourced: the papers could not be fetched): at equal hotel load the glider has the longer best range in 5.9% of cases, at 5 times the AUV hotel load in 89%, so the advantage comes from hotel load rather than hydrodynamics; glider speed tops out at 0.13 to 0.70 m/s, and the proposal's 0.4 to 0.9 m/s crossover is not supported. Not checked against a fielded glider's range. Milestone 4b re-ran it with Slocum aerodynamics read from the MIT-licensed gliderflight package (lift slope 7.5/rad, K 10.5/rad²): the glider out-ranges the AUV in 0 of 2,430 cases at equal hotel load, and the break-even AUV hotel load is a median 4.9 times the glider's (10th to 90th percentile 2.4 to 10.7); hotel loads and pump efficiency remain swept, not sourced. Milestone 4c reads a REMUS-100-class AUV's total power from vendor endurance (1.5 kWh, 12 h at 1.5 m/s to 8 h at 3 kn: 125 to 188 W), subtracts the model's 13 to 21 W of propulsion, and gets a 104 to 175 W non-propulsion load; against it the glider has the longer best range in all 810 x 18 cases. The vendor figures are approximate and mutually inconsistent, and energy per metre ignores that the glider is about seven times slower. Milestone 5 rungs: a lifting-line hydrofoil (all foil coefficients swept) and a Savitsky (1964) planing hull both fail to out-range the 4 m monohull (0 of 2,916 and 0 of 48 cases; range ratios up to 0.25 and 0.14), so they are transit-speed options, not endurance options; no tank data checked. Milestone 5b adds a SWATH rung (two fully submerged parabolic torpedoes on Wigley-form struts, Michell wave drag for torpedoes and struts, 4,374 pairs against the 4 m monohull): the SWATH out-ranges the monohull in none, at its best speed (range ratio median 0.69, best 0.83) or at a fixed 3 m/s (median 0.46), because strut wave drag and wetted area outweigh the torpedoes' small wave drag at 200 kg; torpedo wave drag falls with depth at about 2 k<sub>0</sub> as theory says, but no SWATH tank curve was reachable, and stability and seakeeping are not modelled. Milestone 5d charges panel mass to the battery (areal mass 2, 5 and 10 kg/m<sup>2</sup>, swept, not sourced) and lets the array area vary: where the array cannot carry the boat the full deck is still the best layout in every finite-range case, but the range multiplier falls from a median 2.01 (no mass) to 1.95, 1.83 and 1.64; neutrality at 1 m/s is unchanged at 25.1%, by construction. Milestone 5g runs three speed policies against ten years of daily NASA POWER insolation at five sites: slowing when the pack is under 30% never raises distance (hotel load dominates at 0.5 m/s) but cuts pack-empty days, e.g. 25.4% to 4.2% (slow) and 1.5% (hold) for a 4 m boat at 25 N; above 42 N the deficit is seasonal and policy barely helps. Threshold and slow speed are not swept. Milestone 3b checks the placeholder wave term against five bare-hull tank speeds of a published 2.8 m catamaran (Zenodo 18459868, CC BY 4.0; geometry and water type inferred from the tables): the central model (k = 0.25) is 35 to 43% low at Fn 0.33 to 0.58 and within 10% at Fn 0.72 and 0.79; no single wave scale keeps all five speeds within 20% (best worst-case error 29 to 32%), so the placeholder is not safe for catamarans above Fn 0.3. The programme's survey speeds (Fn about 0.16) are below the data's range, and H3 (Holtrop-Mennen) is untouched. Milestone 3u integrates the DARPA SUBOFF bare-hull equations (Groves, Huang and Chang 1989; 0.699 m<sup>3</sup>, 5.988 m<sup>2</sup>, matching the report) and reads the measured DTMB tow-tank resistance on that area: the bare hull's form factor 1+k is 1.17 above 5 m/s (1.14 to 1.18 over the assumed water viscosity), while Hoerner's streamlined-body formula gives 1.07, about 8% low in total resistance; the bow tripwire's drag is in the measurement and was not separated. Applied to a REMUS-class hull this puts 1+k near 1.15 before appendages, inside the swept 1.1 to 1.3. Reynolds numbers 1e7 to 4e7, not the 3e5 to 5e5 of a REMUS. Milestone 6p tests a wave-powered rung on a fielded vehicle: 1,245 hours of a Wave Glider off Hawaii (2015, NOAA ERDDAP) against nearest-buoy sea state. Speed barely rises with wave height (median 1.05× from ≤1.5 m to ≥2.5 m Hs; a quasi-steady foil model predicts 1.9×), a 30% loss from June–July to August–October is as large as the whole sea-state effect, and the one-parameter model loses to a constant on held-out months. Scaled to the programme’s buoys, a wave-powered glider makes about 33 to 50 km/day, half the solar ceiling. Milestone 6q asks what forecasts that vehicle’s speed: the median of its previous 24 hours predicts held-out speed a day ahead to 0.048 m/s, a third of a constant’s error. Even a perfect sea-state forecast adds no measurable skill on top (error ratio 0.99, 95% interval 0.86 to 1.16), within a month speed scales as about Hs<sup>0.2</sup>, and a time-since-launch trend fails when extrapolated. Milestone 6r carries that into planning: with speed proportional to Hs<sup>0.22</sup> at a fixed vehicle state, the programme’s 2024 buoys give 30 to 61 km/day; the best site over the worst is worth 20% (January) to 34% (July), the 2015 vehicle’s best month over its worst 64%, so a wave-glider plan is set mostly by the vehicle, not the site. Milestone 6s adds wave period at that fixed vehicle state: its exponent is −0.025 (95% −0.27 to 0.17), it adds no forecast skill, and the buoy plan moves by about 1%, so the Pacific’s lead is from wave height. Milestone 6u replaces the buoy, often 100 to 300 km away, with the vehicle’s own on-board wave sensor: the two agree poorly (within-month correlation 0.20), and with on-board waves speed scales as Hs<sup>0.35</sup> (95% 0.30 to 0.42), with a strong period term (exponent −0.71), roughly (Hs/T)<sup>0.53</sup>, a sub-linear power of heave velocity. That overturns 6s’s period null, and post hoc an oracle on-board sea-state term cuts the day-ahead persistence error by a quarter, reversing 6q. Headwind has no measurable effect, and the 7 August step is about 70% vehicle-side. Milestone 6v reruns 6r’s buoy plan with that on-board law: fleet medians 55 (January) and 45 km/day (July) at the vehicle’s best month, 33 and 27 at its worst. In January the best buoy over the worst falls to 1.12 (from 1.20), because the Pacific’s big seas come with long periods; in July it rises to 1.73 (from 1.34), above the vehicle-state ratio of 1.68, but the slow Gulf and Nantucket plans sit 88 to 95% below the mission’s 5th percentile of Hs/T, so they are extrapolations. Post hoc the law is unbiased within 10% down to Hs/T 0.12, on only 35 hours below 0.15. Milestone 6w replaces the on-board sensor with ERA5 reanalysis waves at the vehicle’s position: the within-month correlation of Hs/T is 0.87, the speed exponent is unchanged (0.533 against 0.534) and the monthly km/day plan moves by under 0.4 km/day, so the plan can be made from a wave model anywhere; as a forecast term ERA5 adds about 4% skill a day ahead and 15% at three days. Milestone 6x plans the same vehicle from ERA5 over a 10° ocean grid: 50 to 79 km/day (10th to 90th percentile) at its best month in January and July 2024, fastest in the winter storm belts, and no point reaches the 86 km/day deck-solar ceiling. Against the buoy-measured plan at the 2024 NDBC buoys ERA5 runs about 10% high and ranks the buoys right in July (Spearman 0.93) but not in January (−0.12); post hoc that error is site-dependent calibration of ERA5’s mean period (r 0.99).
